summary: Nodal-line semimetals provide a natural setting to investigate how the geometry of a nodal manifold affects interaction-driven quantum phase transitions. Here, we study the Hubbard model on a cubic lattice supporting either nodal-point (cubic $\pi$-flux model) or nodal-line semimetallic states using mean-field theory, determinant quantum Monte Carlo simulations, and a weak-coupling renormalization-group (RG) analysis. In both cases, antiferromagnetic order develops only above a finite interaction strength, with the nodal-line system exhibiting a smaller critical coupling due to its enhanced low-energy density of states and markedly stronger finite-size effects. For the nodal-point model, the quantum critical behavior is compatible with $(3+1)$-dimensional Gross--Neveu mean-field scaling. In contrast, the weak-coupling RG reveals that the nodal line itself is unstable against interactions: although the Hubbard interaction is perturbatively irrelevant, its second-order self-energy generates a symmetry-allowed relevant term proportional to $U^2\cos k_z$, reconstructing the nodal line into isolated, strongly anisotropic nodal points. This weak-coupling reconstruction is distinct from the strong-coupling antiferromagnetic transition and highlights the role of nodal-manifold geometry in interacting semimetals.

title: Noninvertible Lieb-Schultz-Mattis Constraints and Deconfined Criticality
summary: We derive Lieb-Schultz-Mattis theorems for one-dimensional qudit systems with a class of internal noninvertible symmetries implemented by bilinear phase map operators. We show that any Hamiltonian preserving these symmetries together with translation or inversion symmetry must either be gapless or have degenerate ground states. Unlike conventional LSM constraints based on projective representations, these new constraints arise from nontrivial algebraic relations between the internal and crystalline symmetries. We illustrate this mechanism in a $\mathbb{Z}_4$ qudit model hosting two competing phases that spontaneously break the internal noninvertible symmetry and inversion symmetry, respectively. Numerical simulations reveal a direct continuous transition between these phases, realizing a stable deconfined quantum critical point involving an internal noninvertible symmetry.

title: Probing the Dirac Quantum Geometry in Quantum Magnets from Polarized Raman Spectroscopy
summary: Magnetic Raman spectroscopy is sensitive to quasiparticle quantum geometry, yet microscopic Raman vertices generally prevent a direct geometric interpretation. Here we establish a symmetry-based extraction principle for two-dimensional quantum magnets with two-band quasiparticle excitations. Opposite circular-polarization spectra separate vertex-weighted quantum-metric and Berry-curvature contractions. Near a $C_3$-symmetric massive Dirac valley, symmetry fixes the leading Raman and velocity doublets up to a common scale, allowing the unknown Raman strength and intensity normalization to cancel from their spectral ratio. For an inversion-related pair of massive Dirac cones, the normalized counter-circular Raman asymmetry at frequency threshold $\Omega_{\rm th}$ is fixed by the Chern number and follows a universal near-threshold frequency scaling. This yields a local spectroscopic readout without absolute-intensity calibration or frequency integration. We demonstrate the principle for Majorana fermions in the field-induced honeycomb Kitaev spin liquid and for topological magnons in a honeycomb ferromagnet, and identify the conditions for resolving it experimentally.

title: Thermal and dynamical behaviors of the spin-nematic phases in a spin-1 triangular lattice
summary: The triangular lattice compound Na$_2$BaNi(PO$_4$)$_2$ has been recently established as a strong candidate for realizing the spin-nematic physics. In this theoretical work, we study the finite-temperature properties and the dynamics of a spin-1 triangular lattice model, which reproduces the spin-nematic physics and provides insights relevant to the compound. We show that a small biquadratic interaction can be used for stabilizing the SN phases in the semiclassical approach with SU(3) coherent states, which allows for a mathematical parameterization of the spin-nematic wave functions. With a semiclassical Monte Carlo calculation, the finite temperature transitions into the spin-nematic phases are shown to be related to BKT transitions associated with the proliferation of half vortices in the original spin-1 model. Using quantum Monte Carlo calculations with a low-energy effective model, the phase boundaries are determined and found to agree qualitatively with the semiclassical analysis. Within the spin wave approach, the low-energy spin dynamics can be captured equally well by either the spin-1 model with a small biquadratic term, or the effective spin-$1/2$ model. The accidental degeneracy of the semiclassical approach at zero field is revealed by explicit analytical parameterization, and is shown to be associated with the pseudo-Goldstone mode observed in the spin dynamics.

title: Learning to control and predict light-driven electron-phonon dynamics
summary: Driving lattice vibrations provides a direct route to manipulating electronic correlations through nonlinear electron-phonon coupling. Finding suitable driving fields, however, requires control over the coupled dynamics beyond a simple choice of pulse amplitude and frequency. Here we develop a differentiable framework that combines field optimization with neural-network prediction in a two-site electron-phonon model. We compare piecewise-constant, B-spline, feed-forward, and recurrent control parameterizations, optimized to increase the accumulated electronic double occupation. For the dissipation-free model at zero Hubbard interaction, all the methods increase double occupation, with the B-spline raising the mean total double occupation of approximately 30%. Alongside control optimization, a separate recurrent network learns to predict the next-step double occupation and phonon observables from their preceding values and the applied field. These results establish a computational proof of concept for shaping local electronic correlations through a phonon drive and identify a promising route toward learned models for nonequilibrium materials control.

title: Symmetry-preserving gapped Dirac state revealed by site-selective $^{13}$C NMR in $\alpha$-(BETS)$_2$I$_3$
summary: We report evidence that the low-temperature insulating phase of $\alpha$-(BETS)$_2$I$_3$ preserves both inversion and time-reversal symmetries using site-selective $^{13}$C nuclear magnetic resonance. $\alpha$-(BETS)$_2$I$_3$ undergoes a metal-insulator transition or sharp crossover at approximately 50 K and has been proposed as a candidate spin-orbit-coupling-induced Dirac insulator, yet the nature of its insulating ground state remains unresolved. The NMR spectra exhibit no additional splitting down to 2 K and remain fully described by one quartet and two doublets associated with the three types of molecular sites, A (=A$^{\prime}$), B and C sites, demonstrating the preservation of inversion symmetry. Furthermore, no anomalous line broadening or critical enhancement of the nuclear spin-lattice relaxation rate is observed, indicating the absence of magnetic ordering and time-reversal-symmetry breaking. Analysis of the Knight shifts yields site-specific spin susceptibilities satisfying $\chi_{\mathrm{C}} > \chi_{\mathrm{A}} > \chi_{\mathrm{B}}$, a characteristic feature of tilted Dirac-cone electronic states as observed in $\alpha$-(BEDT-TTF)$_2$I$_3$ under pressure. However, the faint field-induced ferrimagnetic-like spin excitations observed in $\alpha$-(BEDT-TTF)$_2$I$_3$, which are ascribed to the gapless tilted Dirac cones, are absent in $\alpha$-(BETS)$_2$I$_3$. These results demonstrate that the insulating ground state of $\alpha$-(BETS)$_2$I$_3$ is a symmetry-preserving gapped Dirac state and provide microscopic constraints on proposed correlated topological phases in this molecular Dirac system.

title: Unconstrained $\mathbb{Z}_2$ gauge theory on a triangular lattice: deconfined fermions in a vison crystal and superfluidity
summary: We investigate an unconstrained $\mathbb{Z}_2$ gauge theory coupled to fermions on the triangular lattice at half filling, using auxiliary field quantum Monte Carlo simulations. The triangular geometry gives rise to a global $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry that acts as an Ising symmetry on the plaquette fluxes. At weak transverse field $h$, this symmetry is spontaneously broken, stabilizing a vison crystal. We argue that this phase is deconfined: fermions, charged under an emergent $\mathbb{Z}_2$ gauge field, propagate in an ordered $\pi$-flux background and form a Dirac semimetal. Increasing the transverse field triggers a first-order quantum phase transition to a confined $s$-wave superfluid, at which confinement and global symmetry breaking occur simultaneously. This contrasts with the square lattice, where the corresponding transition is continuous. We extend our analysis to finite temperature and determine the thermal phase boundaries of both ordered phases. The superfluid melts through a Kosterlitz--Thouless transition, whereas the vison crystal undergoes a thermal Ising transition. Together, our results establish the $T \times h$ phase diagram and demonstrate how the triangular geometry leads to qualitative changes in both the phases and the criticality of the model.

title: Theory of critical behavior at non-polar structural phase transitions from functional renormalization
summary: $O(N)$ models provide a versatile framework for describing continuous phase transitions in a wide variety of physical systems. We investigate an extension of these models arising from order parameters that transform under interlocked internal and spatial symmetries which describe transitions towards non-polar structural order. Such order occurs, for instance, in dipolar antiferromagnets, spin-orbit-coupled magnets, non-polar ferroics, and certain nematic systems. The resulting effective theory is an $O(d)$ model with an additional symmetry-allowed kinetic term $h(\partial_i\phi_i)^2$, which modifies the relative stiffness of longitudinal and transverse fluctuations. We study both thermal and quantum phase transitions within this $O(d)$ model using the functional renormalization group (FRG). In contrast to conventional $O(N)$ models, the interlocking of internal and spatial symmetries distinguishes spatial and imaginary-time derivatives, such that the quantum model is not simply obtained from the thermal one by a dimensional extension $d\rightarrow d+1$. We derive and analyze the corresponding FRG flow equations, paying particular attention to the tensor structure of the two-point function, which is essential for consistently extracting the flow of the kinetic terms. Our analysis shows that the additional kinetic coupling is irrelevant at the $O(d)$ Wilson-Fisher fixed point in both thermal and quantum cases, where quantum-to-classical correspondence thus re-emerges. However, its small but sizable correction-to-scaling exponent gives rise to substantial corrections to scaling in the vicinity of the critical point.

title: A neural quantum state variational Monte Carlo study of Aharonov-Casher bands
summary: We use neural-network-based variational Monte Carlo to investigate the competition between fractional Chern insulators and generalized Wigner crystals in the Aharonov-Casher Hamiltonian, a continuum model for moir\'e materials. We introduce a variational wave function inspired by flux attachment that captures fractionalized phases and, by comparing its energy with that of a Slater--Jastrow ansatz that captures crystalline phases, we determine the phase diagram at fractional fillings in regimes of strong band mixing and for system sizes beyond the reach of other methods. We find that discrete translation symmetry, encoded in a nonuniform quantum geometry, affects fractionalized states at filling fractions $\nu=1/3$ and $\nu=2/3$ differently, and that band mixing can stabilize incommensurate crystalline ground states. Our results further reveal the delicate competition between topological and non-topological crystalline phases.

title: Reentrant Nematicity from Landau Quantization near a Pomeranchuk Instability
summary: Landau quantization can induce nematic order in a two-dimensional Fermi liquid that is isotropic at zero magnetic field. Using a mean-field theory near a quadrupolar Pomeranchuk instability, we show that varying the magnetic field produces alternating nematic and isotropic regions, with transitions that can be either continuous or first order. The resulting nematic state also leaves distinctive signatures in the de Haas--van Alphen oscillations. At fixed chemical potential, the field-dependent deformation of the Fermi surface can produce substantial changes in the oscillation frequency, even when the cyclotron mass varies only modestly. At fixed particle density, conservation of the Fermi-surface area preserves the leading oscillation frequency, while the cyclotron mass and harmonic amplitudes remain sensitive to nematic order. These contrasting behaviors provide experimentally relevant signatures of field-induced nematicity and reveal the importance of thermodynamic constraints in quantum-oscillation measurements.

title: The de Haas--van Alphen effect in a two-dimensional nematic Fermi fluid
summary: Quantum oscillations are widely used to probe the Fermi surface of metals, but their behavior becomes more complex when electronic interactions can spontaneously deform that surface. We investigate this interplay in a two-dimensional model of interacting electrons capable of developing nematic order, using a uniform mean-field approximation in a perpendicular magnetic field. We show that Landau quantization can favor or suppress nematic order as the field varies, producing alternating isotropic and nematic regions near a Pomeranchuk instability, with both continuous and first-order transitions. Conversely, the evolving nematic order modifies the de Haas--van Alphen oscillations in ways that depend on the thermodynamic conditions. At fixed chemical potential, the oscillation frequency can change significantly even when the cyclotron mass varies only modestly. At fixed particle density, conservation of the Fermi-surface area preserves the leading Onsager frequency, while the cyclotron mass and harmonic amplitudes remain sensitive to nematic order. The magnetization and magnetic susceptibility provide additional signatures of the nematic transitions. These results show how quantum oscillations can both reveal and influence electronic order, offering a framework for interpreting experiments in strongly correlated metals.

title: Lattice response theory for subsystem symmetry-protected topological phases
summary: We develop a framework to study subsystem symmetry-protected topological (SSPT) phases using lattice response theory. We begin with a systematic construction of spacetime lattice gauge fields from general microscopic $X$-type symmetry actions on qudit systems, including global symmetries, subsystem symmetries, and more general modulated symmetries. Given a gauge-invariant response action, we then construct a corresponding entangler and explicitly show that it implements stacking with the SSPT phase described by the response action. We show that a broad class of SSPT phases can be described by intersection pairings and realized by cluster entanglers. We also study SSPT phases beyond intersection pairings, including those described by subsystem analogues of type-II group cocycles involving the Bockstein homomorphism. We construct a new 3+1d SSPT phase protected by two 2-foliated planar subsystem symmetries and a global 0-form symmetry, whose response action is a subsystem analogue of a type-III cocycle. On its boundary, the 0-form symmetry acts by stacking with a 2+1d linear SSPT phase, signaling a mixed 't Hooft anomaly.

title: Optimizing Chern Bands for Moore-Read States: A Parent Hamiltonian Approach
summary: The recent realization of fractional quantum anomalous Hall states in moir\'e materials motivates efforts to stabilize non-Abelian topological order in the absence of a magnetic field. Here, we propose a framework for optimizing interactions to favor the non-Abelian Moore-Read state. Our approach compares band-projected three-particle spectra to that of the Moore-Read parent Hamiltonian, which is defined by a three-body interaction, and quantifies the comparison by defining a cost function that estimates proximity to the ideal Moore-Read limit. We apply our approach to Landau levels and to the Chern bands of twisted MoTe$_2$.

title: Cubic, Non-Fermi Liquid Exchange Couplings for Doublet Impurities
summary: We construct non-Fermi liquid (NFL) quantum impurity models for doublet impurities in a cubic metal, involving conduction electrons with half-integer total angular momentum, $J$. We highlight the only two crystal-symmetry-protected NFL quantum impurity models: the spin-half impurity, $J=3/2$ conduction electron Kondo model, and the two-channel Kondo model originally derived in the context of the quadrupolar Kondo model. We show explicitly that the quadrupolar Kondo model preserves time-reversal symmetry. We also construct two cubic quantum impurity models in which NFL behavior is not symmetry-protected. Each has $\Gamma_8$ and either $\Gamma_{6}$ or $\Gamma_{7}$ conduction electrons screening the impurity simultaneously, one model for a non-Kramers doublet and the other for a Kramers doublet impurity ground state. To our knowledge, the latter model has not been considered before; we expect it to realize a new NFL fixed point, but its solution is left for future work. Finally, we derive the relevant cubic perturbation that drives the non-symmetry-protected systems away from their NFL scaling regimes.

title: Symmetry-Enabled Rolling of Composite Bosons: A Route to Superconductivity from Strong Repulsion with $T_c$ Proportional to the Electron Bandwidth
summary: Motivated by superconductors discovered in systems with a strong Coulomb repulsion, we ask whether such a repulsion can give rise to superconductivity with a transition temperature $T_c$ bounded only by the electron bandwidth. Coulomb repulsion can produce pairing as it binds electrons to holes. If each hole binds three electrons into a three-electron-one-hole (3e1h) composite, the condensation of these bosonic composites can give rise to superconductivity. However, the resulting $T_c$ falls far below the electron bandwidth in the controlled regime where the binding is much stronger than the carriers' kinetic energy. This is because, on a lattice, a tightly bound composite usually has to move through a higher-order process where the intermediate state costs an energy of order the binding energy, so that the strong binding makes the composite heavy, limiting the superfluid stiffness and hence $T_c$. Here, we show that symmetry offers a way around this tradeoff. In lattices satisfying certain symmetry requirements, a composite can move by single-particle hops without any costly intermediate state, a motion we call rolling. Such rolling keeps the mass of the composite finite even for an infinitely strong binding, so that a $T_c$ proportional to the electron bandwidth can be achieved in the controlled regime. We derive a criterion for rolling and apply it to construct all fourteen minimal lattice models that support such rolling. We show that rollable 3e1h composites can indeed be stabilized in the ground state. We then propose to realize such superconductivity in a dual-gate bilayer, and use exact numerics to show that $T_c$ can reach a few percent of the electron hopping. These results establish rollability as a guiding principle in the search for and design of superconductors in strongly repelling electron systems, with the minimal models constructed here as prototypes.

title: Interplay of Pair Density Wave and Uniform Superconductivity on the Kagome Lattice
summary: We study the interplay between pair density wave (PDW) and uniform superconductivity on the kagome lattice within a single-orbital $t$-$W$-$J$ model near the $p$-type van Hove filling, where $W$ and $J$ denote effective pairing attractions on lattice sites and nearest-neighbor bonds, respectively. While onsite attraction favors zero-momentum pairing through the conventional BCS instability, nearest-neighbor attraction naturally promotes finite-momentum pairing due to the kagome geometry and sublattice interference. The model therefore provides a framework for exploring the competition and coexistence between uniform superconductivity and PDW order. Self-consistent mean-field calculations in a $2\times2$ supercell reveal that the uniform component reorganizes both the amplitudes and phase structure of the three $F_1$ PDW components, giving rise to superconducting states absent in the pure bond-pairing limit. A Ginzburg--Landau analysis identifies symmetry-allowed couplings that can favor this reorganization. The resulting states exhibit distinct charge modulations and quasiparticle spectra, while the chiral PDW undergoes topological transitions as the onsite attraction increases. Our results demonstrate how uniform superconductivity reshapes the order-parameter landscape and quasiparticle topology of a PDW state.

title: Evidence of anisotropic surface state residual loss in UTe$_2$ amid isotropic low-energy excitations
summary: We explore the pairing mechanism and possible topological properties of the unconventional superconductor UTe$_2$ through their influence on both the inductive and resistive channels using resonant cavity perturbation techniques. We measure a composite surface impedance for a variety of UTe$_2$ single crystals at microwave frequencies, where the inductive and resistive channels are comparable and can be treated on equal footing. By studying the composite electrodynamics for a large number of resonant modes, we are able to provide a comprehensive picture of the directional dependence of the excitations out of the ground state. We find similar power-law temperature dependencies at low-temperature for both the penetration depth and surface resistance, which in aggregate across modes, are quadratic and isotropic. On the other hand, we find a distinct and systematic anisotropy of the residual loss. The power-law results are inconsistent with a single pair of point nodes on the Fermi surface under weak scattering. We discuss the possibility of topological superconductivity as an interpretation of these isotropic power-laws in conjunction with the anisotropic residual loss.

title: Detrital Remanent Magnetization Analysis at the Particle Scale: Implications for Prebiotic Origins of Homochirality
summary: Detrital remanent magnetization (DRM), the alignment of ferromagnetic grains with the geomagnetic field during sedimentation, is the primary mechanism of paleomagnetic remanence acquisition in sedimentary rocks, yet its microphysical mechanism remains contested. Measured DRM intensities consistently fall below theoretical predictions-the long-standing "DRM efficiency gap"-and no single-particle resolving observations have been available to test DRM acquisition models directly. Here we apply quantum diamond microscopy (QDM) to laboratory-redeposited lacustrine sediments to obtain the first single-particle magnetizations of DRM carriers. We compare these measurements with the results of bulk magnetometry and a Langevin-based kinetic model. We observe a statistically significant mean alignment of individual detrital particle moments with the applied field, $10\%$ when averaged as unit vectors and $24\%$ when weighted by moment magnitude, with the vector sum of all particles reproducing the direction of the bulk DRM, which is $\sim1.8\%$ of saturation remanence. Particle-level analysis shows that alignment rises with particle moment, a trend reproduced by our kinetic model in which floc-hosted magnetite rotates toward the field until the surrounding sediment locks it in place. Even where post-depositional disturbance is minimal and the measured DRM reaches the upper end of reported efficiencies, it remains well below its theoretical maximum, limited in comparable measure by incomplete particle-level alignment and sub-saturation within-particle magnetization. Beyond its implications for the DRM mechanism, this strong particle-level bias provides a quantitative foundation for magnetic minerals as natural chiral agents, a proposed pathway for the emergence of biomolecular homochirality on the prebiotic Earth.

title: Hybrid Machine Learning for Physically Consistent Prediction of Mutual Diffusion Coefficients in Binary Liquid Mixtures
summary: Experimental data on mutual diffusion coefficients in liquid mixtures are scarce, and existing prediction methods are unreliable for non-ideal mixtures. Building on HADES, our hybrid model for self-diffusion coefficients, we introduce the Enhanced Vignes Equation (EVE), which augments the Vignes equation with a deep-set model. Its inputs are molecular descriptors derived from SMILES and activity-coefficient information from HANNA, a machine-learning model for activity coefficients. EVE predicts Maxwell--Stefan diffusion coefficients; the corresponding Fickian coefficients follow from the thermodynamic factor, likewise obtained from HANNA. Trained and evaluated on 2106 experimental data points for 123 binary mixtures, EVE outperforms all available semi-empirical models, halving the mean absolute relative error for mixtures without experimental infinite-dilution diffusion data. Combined with HADES, EVE yields the complete set of self- and mutual diffusion coefficients of a binary mixture from SMILES and pure-component viscosities alone. EVE and HADES are available at https://ml-prop.mv.rptu.de/, and the code is fully disclosed.

title: Potential for helicity-mediated reverse intersystem crossing in boron--nitrogen-substituted polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons with inverted singlet-triplet gaps
summary: The prospect of exothermic reverse intersystem crossing (rISC) in organic chromophores with inverted singlet-triplet (INVEST) excited states has stimulated considerable interest in next-generation emitters. However, realizing efficient spin conversion remains challenging because energetic inversion does not necessarily imply the appreciable spin-orbit coupling (SOC) required for rISC. Here, we investigate direct ${\rm S}_1-{\rm T}_1$ SOC in 85 INVEST candidates comprising 32 azaphenalenes, 7 non-alternant hydrocarbons, and 46 boron-nitrogen-substituted polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (BNPAHs), all previously predicted to exhibit negative singlet-triplet gaps using a correlated wavefunction method at reliably optimized molecular geometries. While the azaphenalenes and non-alternant hydrocarbons exhibit negligible direct SOC, 28 of the 46 BNPAHs display finite coupling. Analysis of molecular geometries and natural transition orbitals suggests that SOC variations depend on molecular topology, orbital orientation, and electronic-state symmetry rather than nonplanarity or excited-state character alone. We estimate direct-rISC rates with a Marcus model, identifying selected BNPAHs with rates approaching $10^7\,{\rm s}^{-1}$.

title: Open Quantum System Embedded in an Optimized Reservoir of Molecules
summary: Open-boundary Quantum Mechanics/Molecular Mechanics (QM/MM) simulation provides a direct way to test whether a quantum subsystem and its surrounding classical reservoir are physically consistent. Here we use this framework to replace a standard flexible TIP3P reservoir by a dipole-renormalized (DR) Amber-compatible three-site water model optimized against a full \textit{ab initio} trajectory of liquid water. The renormalization targets the molecular dipole distribution and adjusts the atomic charges, bonded, and Lennard-Jones interaction parameters through a stochastic optimization procedure. In the case of a large QM region ($\langle N\rangle\approx 440$), where the surface-to-volume ratio is small, the DR reservoir induces, as expected, Grand Canonical statistics for the quantum subsystem. In smaller subsystems ($\langle N\rangle\approx 190$), where the surface-to-volume condition is deliberately less favorable, the same reservoir shows substantially improved molecular consistency with the QM region relative to the non-renormalized flexible TIP3P model. These results show that quantum information at molecular dipole level is crucial for the microscopic physics of liquid water. When this concept is transferred into a classical reservoir, it can be used to extend the reliable regime of adaptive open-QM/MM water simulations even beyond the physically dictated Grand Canonical conditions. \end{abstract

title: HARMONY: an efficient and accurate deep learning framework for prediction of experimental vibrational spectra
summary: Predicting experimental vibrational spectra requires both efficient molecular calculations and a reliable mapping from theoretical vibrations to measured signals. Here we introduce \textbf{HARMONY}, a two-stage deep-learning framework that bridges this gap using harmonic spectra as physical anchors. Equivariant neural networks directly predict atomic forces and spectroscopic tensors for rapid harmonic-spectrum construction, while HarmoNet combines these spectra with molecular topology and measurement metadata to predict experimental infrared and Raman spectra. HARMONY achieves mean cosine similarities of 0.912 for infrared and 0.907 for Raman spectra, with a mean inference time of 2.12~s per molecule, approximately 600-fold faster than the evaluated DFT workflow. Beyond forward prediction, HARMONY improves inverse molecular inference through pseudo-experimental pretraining and spectral verification of candidate structures. Integrating HARMONY and Vib2Mol as scientific tools within a general-purpose agent enables adaptive candidate generation and verification. With molecular formulas provided, the resulting Vib2Mol--HARMONY Agent achieves Top-1 recall of 70.53\% on NIST using infrared spectra and 83.33\% on SDBS using combined infrared and Raman spectra. Fine-tuning with 19 amino-acid controls and eight peptides further increases mean Raman cosine similarity from 0.669 to 0.896 on 15 held-out peptides. HARMONY establishes harmonic anchoring as a practical connection between molecular physics, experimental spectroscopy and adaptive molecular structure elucidation.

title: Stable ring-polymer molecular dynamics without Fourier transforms: a linear-scaling bead-space Cayley propagator
summary: Ring-polymer molecular dynamics (RPMD) builds zero-point energy and tunnelling into classical trajectories and is widely used for bimolecular rate coefficients. At low temperature it requires many beads, and the stiff ring-polymer springs then limit the integrator. The Cayley modification of the free ring-polymer step removes this limit, but it has so far been formulated mode by mode, which requires Fourier transforms of every degree of freedom at every step. Here we show that, in bead coordinates, the Cayley step reduces to one cyclic tridiagonal solve for the midpoint of the step, with a matrix that depends only on the number of beads $P$, the temperature and the time step, and not on the atomic masses. The bead-space step is exactly the normal-mode Cayley map: it conserves the free ring-polymer energy, preserves the free ring-polymer Boltzmann distribution, and is stable for any $P$ whenever $\Omega\Delta t<2$ for the highest physical frequency $\Omega$. A Thomas recursion with a rank-two Woodbury correction solves it in about $18P$ operations per degree of freedom without pivoting, with a condition number bounded by $1+(\omega_P\Delta t)^2$, and the inverse matrix decays geometrically with bead separation, so the step is local in bead index. Implemented in the open-source PyRPMD package, the propagator reproduces normal-mode Cayley to $1.5\times10^{-15}$ for up to 2048 beads and its cost grows linearly with $P$. For direct RPMD (dRPMD), which has so far integrated the springs explicitly, these properties raise the stability limit on the time step 23--29-fold in published low-temperature settings; at \SI{20}{K} with 3072 beads, the Cayley step conserves the ring-polymer energy as well as velocity Verlet does with a time step about ten times larger, while leaving the low-lying internal modes that govern spurious resonances essentially unchanged.

title: Compensated Grid-Based Hybrid Exchange - A Simple, Accurate, Efficient, and Differentiable Recipe for Large-Scale Molecular Systems
summary: A compensated grid-based approach is developed for hybrid exchange in large-scale molecular systems. The method uses a symmetrically overlap-fitted grid-based exchange approach, with fitting performed in the orthonormalized atomic orbital basis. This fitting is augmented with a superposition-of-atomic-densities difference-density (dSCF) partitioning of the exchange energy, yielding the finished compensated grid-based exchange approach. The complete method is found to have orders of magnitude reduction of absolute and relative error properties versus raw grid-based exchange, and remains analytically differentiable. The method is easy to implement and provides efficiency gains over GPU integral-direct techniques for high quality and/or augmented basis sets. Library functions to help users implement the method in their own quantum chemistry codes are provided in the recently-shipped cuEST v0.3 library.

title: Dynamics and Statistical Mechanics of Born-Oppenheimer Auxiliary Velocities
summary: In Born-Oppenheimer (BO) dynamics, auxiliary variables such as electron densities, induced polarization and electrode charges follow stationarity conditions, yet their time derivatives, such as currents, are physical observables. Using Mass-Zero constrained dynamics, we interpret these derivatives as explicit dynamical variables and derive the invariant measure giving their equilibrium statistical properties. We illustrate the framework in constant-potential molecular dynamics, where the electrode-charge velocities reproduce BO current fluctuations and the frequency-dependent admittance.

title: Library of peptides: Analysis of a complex reactive mixture with the use of statistical physics and inference
summary: Self-assembled mixtures enable the exploration of vast chemical diversity, yet characterizing the hundreds of coexisting species they contain remains a major challenge. Standard analytical techniques such as chromatography and spectroscopy produce overlapping signals that cannot be resolved by conventional deconvolution methods, which neglect the concentration correlations imposed by the reactive network. Here, we introduce a framework that bridges statistical physics and analytical chemistry to deconvolute complex self-assembled mixtures from partial spectral data. Inspired by Potts models of protein folding, we express the chemical potential of each compound as a function of a reduced set of parameters-intrinsic building-block energies and pairwise coupling terms between neighboring building blocks in the sequence. Coupling this model with the law of mass action yields equilibrium concentrations across the entire reactive network. The model parameters can be infered by fitting predicted spectroscopic signals to experimentally measured partial data. We demonstrate this approach using dynamic combinatorial libraries (DCLs) of peptides as a model system. Applied to a DCL of 81 peptides, our method resolves the full mixture composition from just 13 overlapping peaks, revealing that lateral couplings dominate the assembly energetics. Beyond DCLs, this strategy offers a general route for analyzing self-assembled systems from partial data and extends naturally to target-driven identification of high-affinity binders.

title: Quantum Boltzmann Equation for Static Correlation with Cumulant Kernel Closure
summary: We present a Quantum Boltzmann Equation for static correlation by mapping the Bogoliubov-Born-Green-Kirkwood-Yvon hierarchy to discrete atomic-orbital matrix mechanics via the Wigner-Weyl isomorphism to evaluate scattering of the correlated two-body cumulant. This Quantum Boltzmann Equation converges to the active-space static correlation limit and preserves pure $N$-representability constraints during the kinetic relaxation. To resolve scaling bottlenecks of explicit two-body cumulant methods, we project the two-body cumulant onto its lowest unitary invariant and evaluate a susceptibility-windowed orbital scattering scale via a single Coulomb-exchange contraction. Relaxing onto a hyperbolic-tangent cumulant attractor through Markovian collisional relaxation yields a parameter-free Quantum Boltzmann Equation Cumulant-Kernel that regularizes derivative cusps without thermal smearing. Using the collinear $\mathrm{H}_3$ exchange reaction, the symmetric $D_{4h}$ square $\mathrm{H}_4$ dissociation, the non-adiabatic avoided crossing in $\mathrm{BeH}_2$, the symmetric bond cleavage of $\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}$, the triple-bond dissociation of $\mathrm{N}_2$, the 11-molecule MR-MGN-BE17 dissociation test set, and the singlet diradical isomers of benzyne as case studies, we show that this kinetic relaxation resolves strong static correlation at zero electronic temperature.

title: Active-space construction in single-fragment coupled-cluster embedding for chemical reactions
summary: We benchmark single-fragment quantum embedding, in which electron correlation---at the level of coupled-cluster theory with single, double, and perturbative triple excitations [CCSD(T)]---is restricted to orbitals associated with a chosen molecular fragment, and the remaining orbitals are frozen at the Hartree-Fock level. We compare several methods for constructing fragment active spaces, and we test their performance on 60 organic reaction energies and three reaction profiles. A common fragment projection operator is used to relate several of the tested orbital constructions. Regional embedding, based on density matrix embedding theory, is shown to give accurate and robust performance when used for both the occupied and virtual active orbitals. For virtual orbitals, fragment-centered projected atomic orbitals and fragment natural orbitals (defined by eigenvectors of a fragment MP2 density matrix) also perform well, but the latter typically retains larger virtual spaces. Composite MP2 corrections yield the largest improvement: combined with fragment natural orbitals, they give average reaction energy errors below 0.3 kcal/mol relative to full-system CCSD(T), with all individual errors below 1 kcal/mol. Reaction profiles show that accurate endpoint energies can conceal substantial barrier errors, emphasizing the importance of approximating omitted correlation.

title: Plasma simulations with adaptive mesh and algorithm refinement
summary: Adaptive Mesh and Algorithm Refinement (AMAR) combines adaptive Cartesian meshes with automatic selection of kinetic or fluid solvers. It was introduced for rarefied gas dynamics and later extended to gas mixtures, particle and lattice-Boltzmann solvers, computational electromagnetics, and multi-phase flows. In weakly ionized plasmas, the species differ by orders of magnitude in mass, velocity, and time scale. This paper describes PAMAR, a plasma extension of AMAR in which electrons, ions, neutral species, and fields can have independent adaptive-mesh solvers, each with its own phase-space dimensionality, refinement criteria, and time step, coupled through a field solver in one executable built on the Basilisk framework. We present two demonstrations. A transient capacitively coupled plasma in argon is simulated with two-stream kinetic solvers for electrons and ions on independent adaptive quadtrees in $(x,v)$. The simulations resolve three electron groups and the time scales of electron and ion kinetics without statistical noise, at a cost between particle-in-cell simulations and fast kinetic models. A sphere at floating potential in a collisionless or weakly collisional plasma is computed with octree solvers in $(r,v,\mu)$ for both species and compared with an exact method-of-characteristics solution. Per-species meshes resolve the cold ions at a tenth of the uniform-mesh cost. Both demonstrations also select the model cell by cell. In the capacitive discharge, a hybrid ion solver is kinetic in the sheaths and fluid in the bulk. Around the sphere, a hybrid electron solver confines the kinetic solver to the loss-cone layer and uses a Fokker-Planck model in position and total energy elsewhere. It conserves particles exactly across the interface and uses 1.6 to 5.3 times fewer cells. We discuss the next steps toward parallel, implicit simulations of higher-dimensional problems.

title: A Diffusive T-Matrix Unifying the Electric and Magnetic Polarizability Tensors in Conducting Layered Media
summary: Electromagnetic induction is used to detect and classify buried and submerged objects, such as unexploded ordnance in soil and on the seabed. A small object is commonly described by its magnetic polarizability tensor (MPT), which is independent of its position and of the sensor. The MPT assumes that the surrounding medium does not conduct. In seawater at extremely low frequency, or in clay at kilohertz frequencies, this assumption fails at depths comparable to the skin depth. The object then also diverts the current induced in the medium, a galvanic response that the MPT omits. We describe the object instead by its transition matrix (T-matrix), which keeps the independence from position and sensor and includes both responses. It is computed once per medium and frequency from a single finite element problem, for any shape and materials. Its inductive block reduces to the MPT when the medium conducts weakly, and its galvanic block reduces to the electric polarizability tensor in the static limit. We test the model against full finite element solutions for a conducting box, non-magnetic and permeable, in a layered sea and in clay over bedrock. Two orders beyond the dipole, it is accurate to within 1.4% over two decades of frequency and for sizes up to 0.7 of the depth, whereas the error of the MPT carried into the conducting medium reaches 91%. Blocks coupling the two responses, contained in neither tensor, contribute up to 13%.

title: On the statistical reliability of chaotic simulations at reduced precision
summary: Reduced-precision arithmetic is increasingly used to accelerate scientific simulation, while AI workloads are driving its growing prominence in hardware design. Yet small arithmetic errors do not necessarily imply accurate statistics. Finite representation limits spatial resolution, while rounding can merge trajectories that should separate in chaotic systems, progressively concentrating probability on a shrinking collection of computer states. This redistribution can distort statistical averages well before periodicity becomes apparent; furthermore, disjoint computational basins can induce an initialisation bias, even when the intended equilibrium statistics are independent of the initial ensemble. We use functional graphs and their transfer operators to connect these pathologies to bounds on statistical bias, the duration of accurate averaging, and the effect of reducing precision. Exhaustive numerical experiments on four chaotic maps, with 1-24 significand bits and the 24-bit endpoint matching IEEE FP32, show how initially accurate ensembles drift towards incorrect statistics, with lower precision often bringing this deterioration forward. Stochastic rounding substantially extends some useful averaging windows but leaves others severely biased. Longer computed trajectories can therefore worsen inferred statistics, and a finite average can outperform the "infinite-time" computer average by orders of magnitude. This exposes a risk of statistically biased inference at reduced precision and provides a further motivation for collecting statistics from ensembles of shorter trajectories.

title: A Magnetic Neuroevolution Potential for Large Scale Spin-Lattice Simulations
summary: Accurately describing magnetic order, lattice vibrations, and their coupling at finite temperatures within a unified framework remains a major challenge in atomistic simulations of magnetic materials. In this work, we develop a magnetic neuroevolution potential that explicitly incorporates magnetic degrees of freedom, establishing a potential-energy description jointly determined by atomic structures and magnetic configurations and enabling unified predictions of atomic forces and magnetic energy gradients. Using CrN, Fe, and FeGe with collinear or noncollinear magnetic configurations as representative systems, we demonstrate that the model outperforms standard neuroevolution potentials without magnetic descriptors in predicting energies, atomic forces, and virials, while yielding equilibrium lattice constants consistent with experimental values. Phonon calculations for different magnetic states show that the model captures lattice vibrational responses to changes in magnetic order. Finite-temperature spin-lattice dynamics simulations further reveal the temperature dependence of magnetic excitation spectra, while calculations of the average atomic magnetic moment versus temperature demonstrate the influence of spin-lattice coupling on magnetic transition temperatures and system-size convergence. For Fe, explicitly including spin-lattice coupling brings the predicted magnetic transition temperature closer to experiment, whereas the difference in FeGe is smaller. Performance benchmarks demonstrate that the method enables coupled dynamics simulations of over two million atoms on a single consumer-grade GPU. By combining magnetic-configuration resolution with high computational efficiency, the framework provides an efficient tool for investigating finite-temperature dynamics and spin-lattice coupling in large-scale magnetic systems.

title: Sphere-based test cases for open boundary simulations in electrostatics and magnetostatics
summary: This paper presents a library of sphere-based test cases for verifying the correctness of open boundary simulations in electrostatics and magnetostatics for computational physics and engineering applications. While the energy in the fields of a single sphere is computed for various source configurations, the energy, force and torque (when applicable) are also computed for a pair of spheres. An extension to electromagnetic momentum is also given for the single sphere, demonstrating its use as a benchmarking metric. Analytical expressions are provided for each test case, from which the validity of a simulation environment can be assessed. The finite element method is used as the example context, and four different open boundary methods are evaluated. Once verified, the simulation is used to visualize the Poynting vector field associated with an electric charge placed near a permanent magnet, a configuration for which no analytical expression is available. Simulation files are made available and all numerical experiments are reproducible with the ONELAB open source software.

title: Multi-domain AAA-least squares methods and applications
summary: A multi-domain AAA-least squares (nAAALS) method is developed for computing rational approximations of harmonic functions defined in the interior and exterior of multiply-connected domains. Three classes of problems are considered: i) multi-domain problems where an unbounded exterior is punctured by multiple singly-connected domains; ii) nested domain problems where one domain contains multiple punctured domains; and iii) quasi-steady time-stepping problems where the nAAALS algorithm is coupled with standard Runge-Kutta schemes to compute the coupled evolution of the multiple domain boundaries. The nAAALS method extends the original AAALS algorithm in two key ways. First, a function $\tilde{S}$ satisfying $\tilde{S}(z)=\overline{z}$ on each domain boundary is approximated using the AAA algorithm, producing simple poles distributed according to both the individual boundary geometries and the global multi-domain configuration. Second, the least-squares framework is modified to accommodate the coupled matching conditions across each domain boundary. The method is applied to problems in vortex dynamics to demonstrate its capability, focusing specifically on vortex patches as a working example: finite-area regions of incompressible, inviscid fluid in rotational flow. The nAAALS algorithm is used to (a) reproduce known vortex patch equilibria, and (b) compute the evolution of new and existing non-equilibrium configurations. The results are shown to be accurate at low computational cost, running in seconds on a standard laptop. Crucially, the nAAALS method is suitable for addressing a broader class of steady and quasi-steady multi-domain problems across disciplines, such as those arising in applied mathematics, mathematical biology, and fluid dynamics.

title: Bayesian determination of structural ensembles from single-particle X-ray scattering images
summary: Single-particle X-ray scattering with free electron lasers records snapshots of individual molecules with femtosecond time resolution and is therefore ideally suited to study structural heterogeneity or molecular motions. Current approaches to determine structural ensembles rely on prior classification of the scattering images, which is error-prone and becomes infeasible for single macromolecules, whose images contain too few coherently scattered photons. Here, we present a Bayesian approach that samples weighted ensembles of electron densities directly from the posterior probability distribution given all scattering images, thereby avoiding classification altogether. We demonstrate our approach in the low signal-to-noise high heterogeneity regime using synthetic scattering data of a small and flexible protein, as well as on published experimental scattering images for the coliphage PR772 virus.
